messages.subject: Re: Underestimating density?
parts:
Michelle, it's impossible to tell what you did do from that
description. Not sure what you mean by a detection probability of 65 -
do you mean 0.65? If you pooled data across the 9 visits, then effort
per point should be 9, when you analyse in Distance. Better to work
with density rather than calculate abundance, but if you do want to
calculate estimated number of birds on your 16 plots, then you would
just multiply density by the plot area: plot area is16 times pi*50^2
assuming your truncation distance w was 50m. Make sure you're working
with the right units - I'm guessing 50 here is in metres, but your
density may be numbers per hectare for example.

For your point counts, you can estimate density, assuming you detected
everything on the plots, as total number of birds recorded (number of
detections times mean cluster size) divided by 9 times the area of the
plots, assuming you pooled data from the 9 visits.

Steve Buckland

Michelle Greve wrote:
> > Hello
> > I am trying to compare the density (abundance) estimated using DISTANCE to the abundance I actually recorded in my point transects.
> > I re-visited the same sites repeatedly (9 times) and included this information in my data sheet. So, after running the analysis, I have done the following:
> >
> > 1. multiply the density estimate (D) by the area of my point transects (pi*50^2)
> > 2. multiply this by the no. of times each transect was vistited (9)
> > 3. and multiply this by the no. of transects (16)
> >
> > Should the result of this calculation not be comparable to: (the total number of records*cluster size) for this species?
> > My problem is that the density I recorded is more than three times greater than the density estimated in DISTANCE. Did I leave something out of my calculation above?
> > The detection probability is 65 and the detection probability curve looks fine.
> >
> > Any help would be appreciated.
> > Thanks,
> > Michelle
